analysis.one_liner: Gives federal civilian workers an 8.7% pay raise in 2024, including a 4% locality increase.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to give federal civilian workers an 8.7% pay raise in 2024 died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised pay for federal civilian workers by 4.7% in 2024, plus an extra 4% locality pay for a total of 8.7%, well above the smaller raise that was ultimately put in place through the normal budget process. It applies to the statutory pay systems covering most federal employees and to prevailing rate (hourly wage-grade) workers. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up. It never received a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, roughly 2 million federal civilian employees would have received an 8.7% raise in 2024, with blue-collar prevailing rate workers covered as well. The raise would have gone to workers at every federal agency, from VA nurses to border and administrative staff, and would have been larger than the 5.2% raise ultimately set for 2024.

how_it_helps.text: Raises basic pay for all federal employees under the statutory pay systems by 4.7% for 2024.
Raises pay for prevailing rate (hourly/wage-grade) federal workers, such as many blue-collar and trades employees, by 4.7% for fiscal year 2024.
Adds a 4% locality pay increase on top, meaning a combined 8.7% raise, helping federal workers keep up with the cost of living.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally, through larger annual federal salary budgets; the raise would add billions in recurring federal spending.

drawbacks.text: An 8.7% raise across all federal pay systems is a large, recurring cost to taxpayers at a time of high federal deficits, and it applies uniformly rather than targeting the lowest-paid or most underpaid federal workers.

The bill overrides the normal annual pay-setting process and the statutory wage survey system for prevailing rate employees, replacing data-driven adjustments with a flat congressional set-raise [S3], which some would argue bypasses the mechanism designed to match federal wages to local labor markets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The raise is a straightforward, meaningful pay increase for people who work for the government, and it addresses real wage erosion from recent inflation. The tradeoff is purely fiscal: it is a multi-billion-dollar recurring cost paid by taxpayers, and critics could argue the same money could be targeted to the lowest-paid and most underpaid federal occupations rather than spread evenly across the pay scale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it never got a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 26, 2023 and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill had 20 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, which was far short of the support needed to advance it without committee and leadership cooperation.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers who would have funded the raise are better off financially, while federal workers are worse off, having received a smaller pay increase than the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; federal workers lost a larger raise

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to give federal civilian employees an 8.7% pay raise in 2024.

for.name: 19 Democratic senators and 1 independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Fetterman, Brown, and Kaine.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed a federal pay raise of this size, and with Republicans holding enough seats to block most legislation, no path to the floor existed without their support.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats or allied independents; no Republican senator signed on, and the bill made no progress in the Senate.

industries.note: The bill's direct beneficiaries would have been roughly 2 million federal workers, who would see an 8.7% raise in 2024. It died, so their pay followed the lower president's budget alternative instead.
The raise would be funded by federal taxpayers through larger federal salary spending. Its failure avoided that cost but also left federal pay subject to inflation.
